input: In this worked example, we are going to look at what happens to the temperature of natural gas when it is compressed in a single-stage compressor. The compressor raises the natural gas from a pressure of 1 bar up to a pressure of 4 bar, and the gas enters the machine at an inlet temperature of 303 K. If the compression is assumed to be isentropic, which is to say that it takes place without any irreversibility, the discharge temperature can be estimated from the inlet temperature and the pressure ratio of 4 using the standard isentropic relation, taking the heat-capacity ratio of the gas to be 1.4. When the inlet temperature of 303 K and the other values are worked through in this relation, the calculation gives a discharge temperature of 450 K. It is important to note, however, that this isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses, which are inevitably present in any real machine. As a result, the measured discharge temperature of the installed machine is higher than the estimated figure, and the value of 450 K should therefore be treated as an idealised result rather than as a prediction of the temperature that will actually be observed in practice. Examples of this kind are commonly used when a compressor is being specified, since the discharge temperature has a bearing on the materials that are selected for the machine and on the cooling that may need to be provided downstream of it.
target: A single-stage compressor raises natural gas from 1 bar to 4 bar from an inlet temperature of 303 K; calculate the discharge temperature on an isentropic basis. The isentropic relation connects the discharge temperature to the inlet temperature through the pressure ratio and the heat-capacity ratio of the gas. With a pressure ratio of 4 and a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, substitution of the inlet temperature of 303 K gives a discharge temperature of 450 K. The isentropic basis is an idealisation: the compression is treated as reversible, and mechanical losses are excluded from the estimate. The installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher than 450 K, as it must be once those losses enter as heat in the gas. The isentropic value is therefore the floor for the discharge temperature of the real machine and not its expected value, and the difference between the two temperatures is the thermal signature of everything the estimate leaves out. A design that has to bound the discharge temperature from above cannot take the isentropic figure as the bound; it takes the measured behaviour of the installed machine, with the isentropic value marking how much of the rise the compression alone accounts for. The relation also shows where the estimate is sensitive: the pressure ratio enters through an exponent set by the heat-capacity ratio, so the result moves with the ratio rather than with either pressure on its own, and a machine raising the gas through a larger ratio in a single stage would return a discharge temperature well above the present figure, which is the reason staging enters real designs.
